Article · Critical literature review and policy design

Ability before access: who medea the AI that reaches the child

The public debate on generating AI in school has been reduced to two options — release or ban. Neither describes the variable that the strongest available evidence points to as decisive: what the adult does while the child uses.

The responsible integration of the generating AI in the founding years is not a function of access to the child to technology, but the interaction between developmental readiness, competence adult, pedagogical mediation, institutional governance and cognitive function attributed to AI within the learning activity.

In short

What is "capacity before access"

Responsible integration of the AI in the founding years is not a function of child access to technology, but the interaction between developmental readiness, adult competence, mediation quality, institutional governance and cognitive function attributed to AI in the activity. Capacity-before-access is presented here as analytical proposition derived from policy comparison — not as a principle already enshrined in the literature.

  • Two domains, not one — Children's education (0–6) and initial Fundamental (~6–13) are not generalised; confusing them invalidates the conclusion.
  • Four layers of competence — capacity, judgment, mediation and governance; literature almost always measures only the first, and by self-perception.
  • Required, not enough — P1 is partially sustainable, P2 is not supported by any revised study, P3 (conditionality) is the strongest.
  • Replacement × magnification — with unrestricted access, − 17% in the final test without AI; with pedagogic guardrails, sustained gain (Bastani et al., 2025, PNAS).

It is the same principle of fail-closed ed AI Agent Engineering, applied to the classroom: the design decides the outcome, not the tool.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What does "capacity mean before access"?

It is the proposition that children's access to the generative AI should be conditioned to the available mediation capacity — adult competence, quality of pedagogical intervention and institutional safeguards — and not just chronological age. The article treats it as an analytical proposition derived from the comparison between political architectures, not as a principle already established by the literature or by any current policy.

Why separate early childhood education from elementary school?

Because they are distinct domains and the evidence of one does not transfer to the other. Early childhood education (ECEC) designates 0 to 6 years, before compulsory schooling, where the direct use of the tool by the child is minimal and the focus is on adult education. The initial Fundamental (about 6 to 13 years) is where Norway published official guidelines per school stage in 2026, and where the child is already in literacy and numeration. Treating them as a single block compromises the validity of inference, because the evidence of one domain does not support conclusions about the other.

What are the four layers of adult competence?

Capability (the teacher knows how the tool works), judgment (knows how to decide when to use, when not to use and for what purpose), mediation (knows how to intervene during use — question, verify, withdraw support) and governance (the institution allows and structure this intervention, with time, infrastructure and policy). Most of the literature measures only the first, in general by self-perception, silencing precisely the layers that the strongest evidence suggests are decisive.

When does cognitive discharge become a replacement?

Unloading operational load can be desirable and release capacity for higher order reasoning; the precise question is when offloading becomes a replacement for the cognitive process that the child needs to develop. In the randomized trial by Bastani et al. (2025), unrestricted access to the model improved 48% performance during practice but produced a result 17% lower than the control in the final test without AI; with guardrails that prohibited delivering the final response, the improvement was 127% and the gain remained.

Does the restriction of smartphones serve as evidence of a generative AI?

Not directly. The risk mechanisms are distinct: smartphone and social networks operate on attention, distraction and social comparison, while generativa AI operates on cognitive production, outsourcing of reasoning and writing. Evidence of device restriction is treated as comparative evidence of policy — useful for understanding how institutional restrictions behave — rather than as causal evidence of AI.

What does the Norwegian policy of 2026 show?

Demonstrates policy design (policy design): a coherent architecture that combines minimum age, previous teaching competence and explicit pedagogical purpose, with almost total restriction between 6 and 13 years and gradual use between 14 and 16 conditioned to teacher competence. It does not demonstrate policy effectiveness (policy effectiveness): it is too recent for longitudinal impact assessment, and no policy in itself constitutes an experiment.

Is teacher training enough to integrate AI with responsibility?

Not according to the literature reviewed. No study supports the sufficiency of teaching competence as an isolated variable, and the I AI Act itself rejects this premise implicitly by requiring institutional supervision for high-risk uses, regardless of the individual competence of the educator. Adult competence is probably a necessary enabling condition; the most likely intermediate variable is the quality of pedagogical mediation.

Delimitation Summary

Two age domains that literature treats as one

"Child Education" (Early Childhood Education and Care, ECECEC) designates international literature, children from 0 to 6 years, before compulsory schooling. O more robust empirical case available to discuss generative AI — Norwegian policy 2026 — falls on the 1st to 7th year of grannskole, approximately 6 to 13 years. It's early elementary school, not early childhood education.

Treating both as equivalents compromises the validity of the inference, because the Norwegian policy is not an ECEC policy. This article separates domains from beginning — and separation changes what each evidence can sustain.

Decomposition Original proposal

"Teaching digital competence" is too wide to be useful

The unique concept of teaching digital competence hides four distinct layers and partially independent. The distinction matters because most literature measures only the first — and generally by self-perception —, silencing exactly the layers that the strongest evidence suggests are the ones that alter the educational outcome.

PARADA 1

Capacity (capacity)

The teacher You know how does the tool work, technical and theoretically?

Typical failure: not knowing the response of a language model can be manufactured.

CHALLENGE 2

Judgment (judgment)

The teacher can decide when to use, when not to use and with which purpose?

Typical failure: master the tool and still introduce it without clear pedagogical purpose.

CHALLENGE 3

Mediation (mediation)

The teacher knows how to intervene during use — question, check, Retreat backup?

Typical failure: allow the child to copy the AI response without Checking or arguing.

CHALLENGE 4

Governance (governance)

The institution allows and structure that intervention — time, infrastructure, politics, supervision?

Typical failure: the teacher has ability and judgment, but the school offers no time, no filters, no support.

A causal chain stronger than "training → better use"

OECD literature on professional development in ECEC does not simply state that teachers need to know technology: it differentiates foundational skills, intensified and specialized, and anchors digital competence in the understanding of the child development. The resulting chain is more defensible because it makes the technological competence subordinate knowledge about the child — no A replacement for him.

Recasting the hypothesis Original proposal

Three propositions that need to be tested separately

Strong formulation — "teacher training is necessary and sufficient" — not survives a serious test because it mixes three statements of different types. Decomposed, they have distinct epistemic status:

P1 · NEED

Without sufficient adult competence in all four layers, responsible integration of the AI Generating is unlikely.

Partially sustainable

P2 · SUFFICIENCY

Sufficient adult competence alone ensures responsible integration of the AI Generative.

Not sustained

P3 · CONDITION

The educational effect depends on the interaction between adult competency, quality of mediation, maturity of the child and design of the task.

The strongest

Separation avoids displaying capacity-before-access as thesis demonstrated. She is. treated, from start to finish, as analytical proposition derived from synthesis policy comparison — not as a principle established in the literature.

Mechanism causal evidence A

The question is not if there's cognitive discharge, but when it becomes substitution

Not all cognitive offloading It's harmful. Downloading may be desirable, temporary, strategic or compensatory — an external resource that reduces operational burden and releases capacity for higher order reasoning. The scientifically accurate question It's another one: when the unloading becomes cognitive replacement?

The most robust causal evidence of the entire revised matrix responds to this in a way operational. The randomized controlled trial of Bastani and colleagues (2025, PNAS), with about 1,000 high school students in Turkey, compared two accesses to the same model. The group with unrestricted access improved 48% during practice and performed 17% lower than control in the final test without AI. The group whose AI was restricted by guardrails pedagogical — instructed never to deliver the answer final — improved 127% during practice and kept the win in the final test.

Policy instrument Comparative evidence

Why cell phone is not a genetic AI proxy

There are seven restrictions in use: total prohibition; restriction of access; restriction by age; context restriction; supervised use; use conditioned to competence previous teacher; and curricularly integrated use. A recurring error in the literature of public policy is to treat evidence about restriction of smartphones as indirect proof about AI. They're different risk mechanisms.

Table 2 · What exactly each technology puts at risk.
Technology Predominant risk mechanism
Smartphone Attention, distraction, interruption, media.
Social networks Social comparison, dependence, exposure to content.
Generating AI Cognitive production, outsourcing of reasoning and writing, task automation.

What evidence of smartphones shows

A quasi-experimental Norwegian study with administrative data found a reduction in bullying and performance improvement among girls without detectable average aggregate effect (force B). A rapid review with meta-analysis of five studies found aggregated effect modest — d A realistic analysis suggested possible worsening for boys and increased disparity of Gender.

The Brazilian parallel

São Paulo Law 18.058/2024 and Federal Law 15.100/2025 restrict devices personal in schools, with pedagogical exceptions and accessibility. Reports institutions indicate improvement of focus and social interaction in the first semesters; less favored communities, the abrupt implementation was associated with behaviors aggressive — isolated restriction, without psychosocial monitoring, does not solve facilities cultivated outside the school.

This evidence prevents us from stating that technological restrictions are simply ineffective — but they do not allow to conclude that restricting generative AI would produce the same effects.

Case study Policy design

Norway demonstrates policy design — not policy effectiveness

Table 3 · Norwegian official guideline per step (Udir/Regjeringen, 2026).
Age range / step Guideline
0–5 years (Domain A) Restriction of leisure screen time (0.5–1 h/day); emphasis on adult interaction No screen intermediation.
6–13 years (1st–7th year, Domain B) As a rule, students no have access to generative AI for work School kids.
14–16 years (8–10th year) Gradual and cautious use, conditioned to which teachers have acquired sufficient competence in advance.
17-19 years Independent use allowed, with expectation of critical learning of the use of AI.

Administrative data (Udir, 2025) indicate that nine out of ten Norwegian schools report having content filters, but the schools themselves report lack of competence institutional to support teachers in the use of AI — which supports the reading that the restriction preceded, and did not follow, the consolidation of teaching competence.

Norway demonstrates policy design: a coherent architecture of age + teaching competence + pedagogical purpose.
Norway no demonstrates Policy effectiveness: that this architecture produces better learning outcomes than alternatives.

No policy in itself constitutes an experiment. The policy of 2026 is too recent for longitudinal impact assessment. What exists is previous and correlated evidence — the 2024 smartphones restriction — which informed the argumentative basis to extend the restriction to AI, but this generalization is policy inference, not given directly.

There is still one detail that hasty reading loses: politics conditions use in the years 8–10 to previous teaching competence, and also maintains age restriction in the years 1–7 regardless of available competence. The actual model is additive, no replacement — minimum age + previous teaching competence + pedagogical purpose explicit. It's not right to describe it as an "age" exchange for "competence."

Comparison Summary

Three governance architectures, not two

MODEL 1

Age restriction

Chronological age as the main safeguard. Example: Recommendation UNESCO at least 13 years of age for educational use of AI generativa.

MODEL 2

Capacity-conditioned access

Age + previous teaching competence + gradual introduction. Example: a Norwegian policy of 2026 for the 8th–10th year.

MODEL 3

Unrestricted / market-oriented access

Technological availability as the main determinant of access. Example: commercial adoption on educational platforms without public policy mediation.

The productive question is not "which model is right?", but: which architecture offers best correspondence between risk, developmental maturity and mediation capacity available in each institutional context?

Test of propositions

What Evidence Sustains — And What It Does Not Sustain

P1 · Need Partially sustainable

The evidence is indirect but convergent: the absence of competent pedagogical design produces measurable damage (Bastani et al., 2025); Norwegian schools without competence institutional indicators indicate risk of acritical adoption; the literature of AI-TPACK shows that isolated technical knowledge does not replace pedagogical-ethical judgment.

Calibrated formulation: adult competence is probably a enabling condition required in many forms of responsible integration, but this need was not tested directly in the domains A and B with generative AI.

P2 · Suficiency Not sustained

No reviewed study directly tests this proposition. EU AI Act itself rejects the implicit premise when requiring institutional supervisory infrastructure — a governance layer — for high risk systems, regardless of competence individual educator.

Calibrated formulation: the current literature does not allow to sustain the sufficiency of teacher training as an isolated variable.

P3 · Conditionality The strongest

The experimental design of Bastani et al. (2025) shows, with strength A, that the presence of of guardrails Education — demonstration of design competence, similar to Judgment layer — substantially alters the effect of AI on the retention of learning in teenagers.

Calibrated formulation: teacher competence may be necessary, but it is difficult to suffice; the most likely intermediate variable is pedagogical mediation — and it is this variable, not "competence" in abstract, that agenda future should prioritize measuring directly.

Template Original proposal

A continuum of governance, not a dichotomy

Instead of the binary axis ban ↔ access, a gradual continuum crossed by an axis Cognitive function transversal — replacement on one side, enlargement on the other — present at any point in the sequence:

  1. Protective restriction Temporary and selective, while capacity does not exist.
  2. Adult capacity building Layers 1 and 2: capacity and judgment.
  3. Teacher-mediated access Layer 3: intervention during use, with progressive withdrawal of support.
  4. Appropriate use of age and development The developmental readiness as a criterion, not the availability of the tool.
  5. Cognitive enlargement Layer 4: institutional governance supporting the process.

The continuum as an operable criterion Original proposal

A continuum that doesn't say what to do on Monday is vocabulary, not governance. A table below is the operable form of the same sequence — and remains proposed: no line it has been empirically validated in the domains A or B.

Table 6 · From the continuum to the decision criterion, per step.
Step Purpose permitted Adult role Minimum Safeguard Criteria for withdrawal of support
0–5 (Domain A) None involving direct use by the child. AI is an adult tool. Form in layers 1 and 2 before any introduction. Human interaction without screen intermediation as standard. It does not apply — there is no support to withdraw.
6–9 (Domain B) Learn about AI as an object, in a mediated and collective context. It conducts activity; the child does not operate the tool alone. No task the AI can generate in full. The child can explain what the tool did and why it can make mistakes.
10–13 (Domain B) Learn with AI in task whose central cognitive work remains of child. It intervenes during use: questions, requires verification, interrupts the copy. Guardrails to prevent the delivery of the final answer. The child demonstrates the result without the tool available.
14–16 Gradual use, conditioned to previous teaching competence. Draw the task and audit the process, not just the product. Pedagogic purpose declared before use, not after. Evaluation without AI maintains the performance obtained with it.

The last column is the one that carries the weight. It is the Bastani test transposed into the room: if the performance does not survive the removal of the tool, what happened was substitution — and none I gain measured during practice denies that.

What conditions of governance and pedagogical design move the use of AI to replace expansion, at each point of the continuum and in each age domain?

The formulation avoids presenting restriction and training as competing policies: a protective restriction can function as a governance mechanism Transitional — without this implying that they are necessarily sequential steps in every context.

What is missing to know

Search Agenda

The gap is not treated here as a problem to be solved by optimistic inference: a literature offers sufficient frameworks to formulate the hypothesis and insufficient to establish causality. Five drawings would close that distance.

1 · four-arm CTR

Adapting Bastani et al. (2025) separately for domains A and B: without AI; AI without mediation; AI with trained teacher in the four layers; AI with qualified teacher and additional restrictions. Outcomes: reading, writing, calculation emerging, autonomy and substitution versus enlargement indicators.

2 · longitudinal study per layer

Separately measure capacity, judgment, mediation and governance institutional, avoiding the recurrent error of measuring only self-perception of the first.

3 · Study of formal mediation

Test the model directly teaching competence in AI → quality of pedagogical mediation → child outcome, with direct observation in the room — no Just questionnaires.

4 · Dose-response and thresholds

Compare 3–5, 6–8, 9–11, 12–13 and 14–16 years, testing whether vulnerability to cognitive replacement varies nonlinearly with age — hypothesis suggested, but not tested, by the very age architecture of Norwegian politics.

5 · Impact assessment of Norwegian policy

When there are longitudinal data, test if the architecture "age + teaching competence + pedagogical purpose" produces better outcomes than others two governance models.

Conclusion

Restriction and training need not be competing policies

The most defensible answer is conditional, not binary. Adult competence — decomposed in capacity, judgment, mediation and governance — is probably a qualifying condition necessary, but no revised evidence supports its isolated sufficiency. A conditionality is the most well supported proposition: the design of the task and the quality of the mediation alters the effect of AI on learning — chain demonstrated in adolescents, not in domain children A or B.

Restriction can function as a temporary governance mechanism until capacity human and institutional for responsible mediation be established. Without that implies that one should always precede the other in every context, or that the combination already has been empirically validated as superior to the alternatives.

This is not a conclusion that "we must use AI in children", nor that "we must I forbid it." It is a conclusion on conditional governance architecture — whose validity Predictive remains an open question.

Main limitation declared

Absence of longitudinal and experimental studies linking teaching competence, mediation quality and infant outcomes specifically with generating AI in both age areas defined. Every statement above is calibrated by this absence.

The same principle governs a reliable AI agent on another scale: stop at a safe point Instead of promoting a hunch. View AI Agent Engineering and, about when to stop to refine a problem, Problem Formulation.
